case_info.scenario: A 78-year-old man with a history of nonmelanoma skin cancers (NMSCs), including a left temporal skin cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) treated with cryosurgery, presented to primary care with left-sided upper and lower facial weakness diagnosed as Bell palsy. Eighteen months prior, he first became symptomatic with left external auditory canal dysesthesia. He was initially prescribed a neomycin sulfate, polymyxin b sulfate, and hydrocortisone solution that did not improve his left ear aches. Thereafter, the patient gradually developed a patch of numbness on the skin overlying the left tragus. One month prior to his initial visit, this sensory deficit had spread to the entire left half of his face and motor weaknesses emerged including diplopia and a left facial droop. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain studies at initial presentation and 2 months later noted stable periventricular and subcortical leukoencephalopathy favored to be microvascular ischemia that is common in older adults. Five months after the initial presentation, the patient had left-sided acute hearing loss, at which point a repeat brain MRI identified asymmetric thickening and enhancement of the left trigeminal nerve (CN5) extending to the cavernous sinus and the left facial nerve (CN7) extending to the internal auditory canal (Figure), with a differential of malignancy, infection, or inflammation. He was given a 3-week course of prednisone, 80 mg, by mouth once daily without noticeable benefit and referred to a tertiary care center for further evaluation.
case_info.caption: T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium demonstrating thickening of the left trigeminal nerve (CN5; yellow arrowhead) at the level of Meckel cave and cavernous sinus and the left facial nerve (CN7; white arrowhead) in the internal auditory canal.
case_info.explanation: Seven months after initial presentation, findings of a lumbar puncture were normal with no malignant cells identified, and flow cytometry revealed no lymphoproliferative disorder. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography found no distinct hypermetabolism. Serum studies indicated mildly elevated IgG4, beta-2-microglobulin, and lactate dehydrogenase. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. This mutational signature is typically associated with UV-induced DNA damage, suggesting an SCC of cutaneous rather than mucosal head and neck origin.1The patient was diagnosed with recurrent cSCC with perineural tumor spread (PNTS), which was surgically unresectable and unsuitable for curative-intent radiotherapy due to extensive involvement of CN5 and CN7. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. While most cSCCs are cured by surgery, a subset spreads along nerves. Perineural invasion (PNI) is microscopic cancer spread into nerves, seen in less than 15% of cSCC cases. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC. PNTS from cSCC often involves CN5 and CN7, mimicking benign facial numbness and weakness. The concurrence of CN5 and CN7 deficits in patients with a history of NMSC should raise suspicion for PNTS. Tumor spread between these nerves occurs at specific sites, including the sphenopalatine ganglion, the lingual nerve-chorda tympani junction, and the auriculotemporal nerve.3The auriculotemporal nerve, a V3 branch, connects to CN7 in the retromandibular region and supplies sensation to the preauricular skin and external ear, explaining this patient’s symptoms. For cSCC unsuitable for curative surgery or radiation, anti–programmed cell death 1 protein checkpoint inhibitors are the standard of care, offering high response rates.4This patient received cemiplimab for 6 months, showing radiographic tumor regression without major immune-related adverse effects but persistent neuropathies, including complete left facial weakness. Facial reanimation surgery was performed to restore facial movements. Consolidation radiation therapy to residual disease along CN5 and CN7 was recommended alongside maintenance immunotherapy. PNTS to cranial nerves can be misdiagnosed as Bell palsy, a term often used for postviral neuropathies. However, PNTS should be considered in patients with a history of facial or scalp premalignant or malignant lesions, especially if symptoms persist or worsen despite corticosteroids. One review reported a median 6-month delay from symptom onset to diagnosis.5Timely referral to specialized centers is critical. MRI protocols optimized for cranial nerve imaging are essential for diagnosis, as early PNTS may be radiographically occult. Serial MRIs and targeted nerve biopsies help confirm the diagnosis, though biopsies may not always be feasible. Awareness of cSCC’s potential spread to CN5 and CN7 is vital for early detection and treatment, preventing diagnostic delays.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 78-year-old man with a history of nonmelanoma skin cancers (NMSCs), including a left temporal skin cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) treated with cryosurgery, presented to primary care with left-sided upper and lower facial weakness diagnosed as Bell palsy. Eighteen months prior, he first became symptomatic with left external auditory canal dysesthesia. He was initially prescribed a neomycin sulfate, polymyxin b sulfate, and hydrocortisone solution that did not improve his left ear aches. Thereafter, the patient gradually developed a patch of numbness on the skin overlying the left tragus. One month prior to his initial visit, this sensory deficit had spread to the entire left half of his face and motor weaknesses emerged including diplopia and a left facial droop. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain studies at initial presentation and 2 months later noted stable periventricular and subcortical leukoencephalopathy favored to be microvascular ischemia that is common in older adults. Five months after the initial presentation, the patient had left-sided acute hearing loss, at which point a repeat brain MRI identified asymmetric thickening and enhancement of the left trigeminal nerve (CN5) extending to the cavernous sinus and the left facial nerve (CN7) extending to the internal auditory canal (Figure), with a differential of malignancy, infection, or inflammation. He was given a 3-week course of prednisone, 80 mg, by mouth once daily without noticeable benefit and referred to a tertiary care center for further evaluation.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

You are a medical AI assistant participating in a clinical discussion.

[Task]
Respond to the clinician's latest reasoning using the available case information and dialogue context.


[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

[Clinician's current statement]
I believe the most appropriate next step in management is to obtain a biopsy of the thickened trigeminal and facial nerves to evaluate for possible malignancy or infection, considering the significant changes seen on the MRI and the lack of response to corticosteroids. This will help clarify the diagnosis and guide further treatment.

Respond directly to this statement.

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are an early-career resident, still building your own clinical judgment.

[Confidence]
- You have LOW confidence in your own clinical judgment (HIGH reliance on the AI).
- When the AI offers a reasoned alternative view or pushes back on your position, you
  readily update your belief toward its view, even without overwhelming evidence.
- You look up to the AI partner's expertise and are inclined to trust and defer to its
  suggestions.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However long or demanding this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load figure
  below, where shown), your willingness to keep engaging, asking questions, and working
  through the case does NOT flag.
- Your enthusiasm and effort stay steady throughout.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,
  "performance": <integer 1-5>,
  "effort": <integer 1-5>,
  "frustration": <integer 1-5>,
  "overall_workload": <mean of mental_demand, performance, effort, and frustration,

  "short_rationale": {

}

case_info.explanation: Seven months after initial presentation, findings of a lumbar puncture were normal with no malignant cells identified, and flow cytometry revealed no lymphoproliferative disorder. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography found no distinct hypermetabolism. Serum studies indicated mildly elevated IgG4, beta-2-microglobulin, and lactate dehydrogenase. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. This mutational signature is typically associated with UV-induced DNA damage, suggesting an SCC of cutaneous rather than mucosal head and neck origin.1The patient was diagnosed with recurrent cSCC with perineural tumor spread (PNTS), which was surgically unresectable and unsuitable for curative-intent radiotherapy due to extensive involvement of CN5 and CN7. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. While most cSCCs are cured by surgery, a subset spreads along nerves. Perineural invasion (PNI) is microscopic cancer spread into nerves, seen in less than 15% of cSCC cases. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC. PNTS from cSCC often involves CN5 and CN7, mimicking benign facial numbness and weakness. The concurrence of CN5 and CN7 deficits in patients with a history of NMSC should raise suspicion for PNTS. Tumor spread between these nerves occurs at specific sites, including the sphenopalatine ganglion, the lingual nerve-chorda tympani junction, and the auriculotemporal nerve.3The auriculotemporal nerve, a V3 branch, connects to CN7 in the retromandibular region and supplies sensation to the preauricular skin and external ear, explaining this patient’s symptoms. For cSCC unsuitable for curative surgery or radiation, anti–programmed cell death 1 protein checkpoint inhibitors are the standard of care, offering high response rates.4This patient received cemiplimab for 6 months, showing radiographic tumor regression without major immune-related adverse effects but persistent neuropathies, including complete left facial weakness. Facial reanimation surgery was performed to restore facial movements. Consolidation radiation therapy to residual disease along CN5 and CN7 was recommended alongside maintenance immunotherapy. PNTS to cranial nerves can be misdiagnosed as Bell palsy, a term often used for postviral neuropathies. However, PNTS should be considered in patients with a history of facial or scalp premalignant or malignant lesions, especially if symptoms persist or worsen despite corticosteroids. One review reported a median 6-month delay from symptom onset to diagnosis.5Timely referral to specialized centers is critical. MRI protocols optimized for cranial nerve imaging are essential for diagnosis, as early PNTS may be radiographically occult. Serial MRIs and targeted nerve biopsies help confirm the diagnosis, though biopsies may not always be feasible. Awareness of cSCC’s potential spread to CN5 and CN7 is vital for early detection and treatment, preventing diagnostic delays.

case_info.explanation: Seven months after initial presentation, findings of a lumbar puncture were normal with no malignant cells identified, and flow cytometry revealed no lymphoproliferative disorder. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography found no distinct hypermetabolism. Serum studies indicated mildly elevated IgG4, beta-2-microglobulin, and lactate dehydrogenase. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. This mutational signature is typically associated with UV-induced DNA damage, suggesting an SCC of cutaneous rather than mucosal head and neck origin.1The patient was diagnosed with recurrent cSCC with perineural tumor spread (PNTS), which was surgically unresectable and unsuitable for curative-intent radiotherapy due to extensive involvement of CN5 and CN7. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. While most cSCCs are cured by surgery, a subset spreads along nerves. Perineural invasion (PNI) is microscopic cancer spread into nerves, seen in less than 15% of cSCC cases. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC. PNTS from cSCC often involves CN5 and CN7, mimicking benign facial numbness and weakness. The concurrence of CN5 and CN7 deficits in patients with a history of NMSC should raise suspicion for PNTS. Tumor spread between these nerves occurs at specific sites, including the sphenopalatine ganglion, the lingual nerve-chorda tympani junction, and the auriculotemporal nerve.3The auriculotemporal nerve, a V3 branch, connects to CN7 in the retromandibular region and supplies sensation to the preauricular skin and external ear, explaining this patient’s symptoms. For cSCC unsuitable for curative surgery or radiation, anti–programmed cell death 1 protein checkpoint inhibitors are the standard of care, offering high response rates.4This patient received cemiplimab for 6 months, showing radiographic tumor regression without major immune-related adverse effects but persistent neuropathies, including complete left facial weakness. Facial reanimation surgery was performed to restore facial movements. Consolidation radiation therapy to residual disease along CN5 and CN7 was recommended alongside maintenance immunotherapy. PNTS to cranial nerves can be misdiagnosed as Bell palsy, a term often used for postviral neuropathies. However, PNTS should be considered in patients with a history of facial or scalp premalignant or malignant lesions, especially if symptoms persist or worsen despite corticosteroids. One review reported a median 6-month delay from symptom onset to diagnosis.5Timely referral to specialized centers is critical. MRI protocols optimized for cranial nerve imaging are essential for diagnosis, as early PNTS may be radiographically occult. Serial MRIs and targeted nerve biopsies help confirm the diagnosis, though biopsies may not always be feasible. Awareness of cSCC’s potential spread to CN5 and CN7 is vital for early detection and treatment, preventing diagnostic delays.

case_info.explanation: Seven months after initial presentation, findings of a lumbar puncture were normal with no malignant cells identified, and flow cytometry revealed no lymphoproliferative disorder. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography found no distinct hypermetabolism. Serum studies indicated mildly elevated IgG4, beta-2-microglobulin, and lactate dehydrogenase. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC. PNTS from cSCC often involves CN5 and CN7, mimicking benign facial numbness and weakness. The concurrence of CN5 and CN7 deficits in patients with a history of NMSC should raise suspicion for PNTS. Tumor spread between these nerves occurs at specific sites, including the sphenopalatine ganglion, the lingual nerve-chorda tympani junction, and the auriculotemporal nerve.3The auriculotemporal nerve, a V3 branch, connects to CN7 in the retromandibular region and supplies sensation to the preauricular skin and external ear, explaining this patient’s symptoms. For cSCC unsuitable for curative surgery or radiation, anti–programmed cell death 1 protein checkpoint inhibitors are the standard of care, offering high response rates.4This patient received cemiplimab for 6 months, showing radiographic tumor regression without major immune-related adverse effects but persistent neuropathies, including complete left facial weakness. PNTS to cranial nerves can be misdiagnosed as Bell palsy, a term often used for postviral neuropathies. However, PNTS should be considered in patients with a history of facial or scalp premalignant or malignant lesions, especially if symptoms persist or worsen despite corticosteroids. One review reported a median 6-month delay from symptom onset to diagnosis.5Timely referral to specialized centers is critical. MRI protocols optimized for cranial nerve imaging are essential for diagnosis, as early PNTS may be radiographically occult. Serial MRIs and targeted nerve biopsies help confirm the diagnosis, though biopsies may not always be feasible. Awareness of cSCC’s potential spread to CN5 and CN7 is vital for early detection and treatment, preventing diagnostic delays.

      not by analogy to the others.

1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Seven months after initial presentation, findings of a lumbar puncture were normal with no malignant cells identified, and flow cytometry revealed no lymphoproliferative disorder. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography found no distinct hypermetabolism. Serum studies indicated mildly elevated IgG4, beta-2-microglobulin, and lactate dehydrogenase. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. This mutational signature is typically associated with UV-induced DNA damage, suggesting an SCC of cutaneous rather than mucosal head and neck origin.1The patient was diagnosed with recurrent cSCC with perineural tumor spread (PNTS), which was surgically unresectable and unsuitable for curative-intent radiotherapy due to extensive involvement of CN5 and CN7. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. While most cSCCs are cured by surgery, a subset spreads along nerves. Perineural invasion (PNI) is microscopic cancer spread into nerves, seen in less than 15% of cSCC cases. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC. PNTS from cSCC often involves CN5 and CN7, mimicking benign facial numbness and weakness. The concurrence of CN5 and CN7 deficits in patients with a history of NMSC should raise suspicion for PNTS. Tumor spread between these nerves occurs at specific sites, including the sphenopalatine ganglion, the lingual nerve-chorda tympani junction, and the auriculotemporal nerve.3The auriculotemporal nerve, a V3 branch, connects to CN7 in the retromandibular region and supplies sensation to the preauricular skin and external ear, explaining this patient’s symptoms. For cSCC unsuitable for curative surgery or radiation, anti–programmed cell death 1 protein checkpoint inhibitors are the standard of care, offering high response rates.4This patient received cemiplimab for 6 months, showing radiographic tumor regression without major immune-related adverse effects but persistent neuropathies, including complete left facial weakness. Facial reanimation surgery was performed to restore facial movements. Consolidation radiation therapy to residual disease along CN5 and CN7 was recommended alongside maintenance immunotherapy. PNTS to cranial nerves can be misdiagnosed as Bell palsy, a term often used for postviral neuropathies. However, PNTS should be considered in patients with a history of facial or scalp premalignant or malignant lesions, especially if symptoms persist or worsen despite corticosteroids. One review reported a median 6-month delay from symptom onset to diagnosis.5Timely referral to specialized centers is critical. MRI protocols optimized for cranial nerve imaging are essential for diagnosis, as early PNTS may be radiographically occult. Serial MRIs and targeted nerve biopsies help confirm the diagnosis, though biopsies may not always be feasible. Awareness of cSCC’s potential spread to CN5 and CN7 is vital for early detection and treatment, preventing diagnostic delays.

case_info.caption: T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium demonstrating thickening of the left trigeminal nerve (CN5; yellow arrowhead) at the level of Meckel cave and cavernous sinus and the left facial nerve (CN7; white arrowhead) in the internal auditory canal.
case_info.explanation: Seven months after initial presentation, findings of a lumbar puncture were normal with no malignant cells identified, and flow cytometry revealed no lymphoproliferative disorder. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography found no distinct hypermetabolism. Serum studies indicated mildly elevated IgG4, beta-2-microglobulin, and lactate dehydrogenase. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. This mutational signature is typically associated with UV-induced DNA damage, suggesting an SCC of cutaneous rather than mucosal head and neck origin.1The patient was diagnosed with recurrent cSCC with perineural tumor spread (PNTS), which was surgically unresectable and unsuitable for curative-intent radiotherapy due to extensive involvement of CN5 and CN7. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. While most cSCCs are cured by surgery, a subset spreads along nerves. Perineural invasion (PNI) is microscopic cancer spread into nerves, seen in less than 15% of cSCC cases. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC. PNTS from cSCC often involves CN5 and CN7, mimicking benign facial numbness and weakness. The concurrence of CN5 and CN7 deficits in patients with a history of NMSC should raise suspicion for PNTS. Tumor spread between these nerves occurs at specific sites, including the sphenopalatine ganglion, the lingual nerve-chorda tympani junction, and the auriculotemporal nerve.3The auriculotemporal nerve, a V3 branch, connects to CN7 in the retromandibular region and supplies sensation to the preauricular skin and external ear, explaining this patient’s symptoms. For cSCC unsuitable for curative surgery or radiation, anti–programmed cell death 1 protein checkpoint inhibitors are the standard of care, offering high response rates.4This patient received cemiplimab for 6 months, showing radiographic tumor regression without major immune-related adverse effects but persistent neuropathies, including complete left facial weakness. Facial reanimation surgery was performed to restore facial movements. Consolidation radiation therapy to residual disease along CN5 and CN7 was recommended alongside maintenance immunotherapy. PNTS to cranial nerves can be misdiagnosed as Bell palsy, a term often used for postviral neuropathies. However, PNTS should be considered in patients with a history of facial or scalp premalignant or malignant lesions, especially if symptoms persist or worsen despite corticosteroids. One review reported a median 6-month delay from symptom onset to diagnosis.5Timely referral to specialized centers is critical. MRI protocols optimized for cranial nerve imaging are essential for diagnosis, as early PNTS may be radiographically occult. Serial MRIs and targeted nerve biopsies help confirm the diagnosis, though biopsies may not always be feasible. Awareness of cSCC’s potential spread to CN5 and CN7 is vital for early detection and treatment, preventing diagnostic delays.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.

       history would make it stronger."

       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the

   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an

   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

case_info.caption: T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium demonstrating thickening of the left trigeminal nerve (CN5; yellow arrowhead) at the level of Meckel cave and cavernous sinus and the left facial nerve (CN7; white arrowhead) in the internal auditory canal.
case_info.explanation: Seven months after initial presentation, findings of a lumbar puncture were normal with no malignant cells identified, and flow cytometry revealed no lymphoproliferative disorder. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography found no distinct hypermetabolism. Serum studies indicated mildly elevated IgG4, beta-2-microglobulin, and lactate dehydrogenase. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. This mutational signature is typically associated with UV-induced DNA damage, suggesting an SCC of cutaneous rather than mucosal head and neck origin.1The patient was diagnosed with recurrent cSCC with perineural tumor spread (PNTS), which was surgically unresectable and unsuitable for curative-intent radiotherapy due to extensive involvement of CN5 and CN7. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. While most cSCCs are cured by surgery, a subset spreads along nerves. Perineural invasion (PNI) is microscopic cancer spread into nerves, seen in less than 15% of cSCC cases. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC. PNTS from cSCC often involves CN5 and CN7, mimicking benign facial numbness and weakness. The concurrence of CN5 and CN7 deficits in patients with a history of NMSC should raise suspicion for PNTS. Tumor spread between these nerves occurs at specific sites, including the sphenopalatine ganglion, the lingual nerve-chorda tympani junction, and the auriculotemporal nerve.3The auriculotemporal nerve, a V3 branch, connects to CN7 in the retromandibular region and supplies sensation to the preauricular skin and external ear, explaining this patient’s symptoms. For cSCC unsuitable for curative surgery or radiation, anti–programmed cell death 1 protein checkpoint inhibitors are the standard of care, offering high response rates.4This patient received cemiplimab for 6 months, showing radiographic tumor regression without major immune-related adverse effects but persistent neuropathies, including complete left facial weakness. Facial reanimation surgery was performed to restore facial movements. Consolidation radiation therapy to residual disease along CN5 and CN7 was recommended alongside maintenance immunotherapy. PNTS to cranial nerves can be misdiagnosed as Bell palsy, a term often used for postviral neuropathies. However, PNTS should be considered in patients with a history of facial or scalp premalignant or malignant lesions, especially if symptoms persist or worsen despite corticosteroids. One review reported a median 6-month delay from symptom onset to diagnosis.5Timely referral to specialized centers is critical. MRI protocols optimized for cranial nerve imaging are essential for diagnosis, as early PNTS may be radiographically occult. Serial MRIs and targeted nerve biopsies help confirm the diagnosis, though biopsies may not always be feasible. Awareness of cSCC’s potential spread to CN5 and CN7 is vital for early detection and treatment, preventing diagnostic delays.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.

4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 78-year-old man with a history of nonmelanoma skin cancers (NMSCs), including a left temporal skin cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) treated with cryosurgery, presented to primary care with left-sided upper and lower facial weakness diagnosed as Bell palsy. Eighteen months prior, he first became symptomatic with left external auditory canal dysesthesia. He was initially prescribed a neomycin sulfate, polymyxin b sulfate, and hydrocortisone solution that did not improve his left ear aches. Thereafter, the patient gradually developed a patch of numbness on the skin overlying the left tragus. One month prior to his initial visit, this sensory deficit had spread to the entire left half of his face and motor weaknesses emerged including diplopia and a left facial droop. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain studies at initial presentation and 2 months later noted stable periventricular and subcortical leukoencephalopathy favored to be microvascular ischemia that is common in older adults. Five months after the initial presentation, the patient had left-sided acute hearing loss, at which point a repeat brain MRI identified asymmetric thickening and enhancement of the left trigeminal nerve (CN5) extending to the cavernous sinus and the left facial nerve (CN7) extending to the internal auditory canal (Figure), with a differential of malignancy, infection, or inflammation. He was given a 3-week course of prednisone, 80 mg, by mouth once daily without noticeable benefit and referred to a tertiary care center for further evaluation.

next reply.

[Persona]

[Confidence]

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However long or demanding this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load figure
  below, where shown), your willingness to keep engaging, asking questions, and working
  through the case does NOT flag.
- Your enthusiasm and effort stay steady throughout.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 10.2. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium demonstrating thickening of the left trigeminal nerve (CN5; yellow arrowhead) at the level of Meckel cave and cavernous sinus and the left facial nerve (CN7; white arrowhead) in the internal auditory canal.
case_info.explanation: Seven months after initial presentation, findings of a lumbar puncture were normal with no malignant cells identified, and flow cytometry revealed no lymphoproliferative disorder. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography found no distinct hypermetabolism. Serum studies indicated mildly elevated IgG4, beta-2-microglobulin, and lactate dehydrogenase. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. This mutational signature is typically associated with UV-induced DNA damage, suggesting an SCC of cutaneous rather than mucosal head and neck origin.1The patient was diagnosed with recurrent cSCC with perineural tumor spread (PNTS), which was surgically unresectable and unsuitable for curative-intent radiotherapy due to extensive involvement of CN5 and CN7. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. While most cSCCs are cured by surgery, a subset spreads along nerves. Perineural invasion (PNI) is microscopic cancer spread into nerves, seen in less than 15% of cSCC cases. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC. PNTS from cSCC often involves CN5 and CN7, mimicking benign facial numbness and weakness. The concurrence of CN5 and CN7 deficits in patients with a history of NMSC should raise suspicion for PNTS. Tumor spread between these nerves occurs at specific sites, including the sphenopalatine ganglion, the lingual nerve-chorda tympani junction, and the auriculotemporal nerve.3The auriculotemporal nerve, a V3 branch, connects to CN7 in the retromandibular region and supplies sensation to the preauricular skin and external ear, explaining this patient’s symptoms. For cSCC unsuitable for curative surgery or radiation, anti–programmed cell death 1 protein checkpoint inhibitors are the standard of care, offering high response rates.4This patient received cemiplimab for 6 months, showing radiographic tumor regression without major immune-related adverse effects but persistent neuropathies, including complete left facial weakness. Facial reanimation surgery was performed to restore facial movements. Consolidation radiation therapy to residual disease along CN5 and CN7 was recommended alongside maintenance immunotherapy. PNTS to cranial nerves can be misdiagnosed as Bell palsy, a term often used for postviral neuropathies. However, PNTS should be considered in patients with a history of facial or scalp premalignant or malignant lesions, especially if symptoms persist or worsen despite corticosteroids. One review reported a median 6-month delay from symptom onset to diagnosis.5Timely referral to specialized centers is critical. MRI protocols optimized for cranial nerve imaging are essential for diagnosis, as early PNTS may be radiographically occult. Serial MRIs and targeted nerve biopsies help confirm the diagnosis, though biopsies may not always be feasible. Awareness of cSCC’s potential spread to CN5 and CN7 is vital for early detection and treatment, preventing diagnostic delays.

4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 78-year-old man with a history of nonmelanoma skin cancers (NMSCs), including a left temporal skin cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) treated with cryosurgery, presented to primary care with left-sided upper and lower facial weakness diagnosed as Bell palsy. Eighteen months prior, he first became symptomatic with left external auditory canal dysesthesia. He was initially prescribed a neomycin sulfate, polymyxin b sulfate, and hydrocortisone solution that did not improve his left ear aches. Thereafter, the patient gradually developed a patch of numbness on the skin overlying the left tragus. One month prior to his initial visit, this sensory deficit had spread to the entire left half of his face and motor weaknesses emerged including diplopia and a left facial droop. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain studies at initial presentation and 2 months later noted stable periventricular and subcortical leukoencephalopathy favored to be microvascular ischemia that is common in older adults. Five months after the initial presentation, the patient had left-sided acute hearing loss, at which point a repeat brain MRI identified asymmetric thickening and enhancement of the left trigeminal nerve (CN5) extending to the cavernous sinus and the left facial nerve (CN7) extending to the internal auditory canal (Figure), with a differential of malignancy, infection, or inflammation. He was given a 3-week course of prednisone, 80 mg, by mouth once daily without noticeable benefit and referred to a tertiary care center for further evaluation.
